newsitem.title: USA: Industry leader sees fewer top muni mart players.
newsitem.headline: Industry leader sees fewer top muni mart players.

text.p: No more major securities firms will exit the municipal bond business in the next few years, but business will be concentrated among eight or fewer firms, Terry Atkinson, managing director of PaineWebber Incorporated, told bond dealers Saturday.
Atkinson, speaking at the 21st annual meeting of Public Securities Association here, was responding to a question on whether he thinks the "shakeout" in the muni industry in recent years is over.
Several key firms stunned market players in recent years by exiting the market, including Salomon Brothers, Credit Suisse First Boston and others.
"Is the shakeout over?" Atkinson said. "I don't necessarily think it's over. But if market volume stays where it has been the last couple of years, it certainly has stabilized and tempered."

Atkinson said, "I don't expect any major current municipal players to leave the marketplace, but I also don't expect any major players to come back into the marketplace." He also said it is unlikely that any major foreign firms will enter the market.
Atkinson said while no major firms will leave the market, the market will get "highly concentrated."
"Historically, the top 10 firms (doing negotiated business) represented about 65 percent of all new issuance," Atkinson said.

"I think you are going to see that seven or eight firms will have 65 to 70 percent between now and the end of the century," he said. He said the figure could be as high as 75 percent and the number of dominant firms could slide below seven.
Atkinson was asked whether the "growing problem of illiquidity" in the muni market will threaten its future.

"There's no question it's a relatively illiquid product," Atkinson said. "There's not that many people making a marketplace. Everytime somebody like a First Boston leaves the market it makes it even more of a challenge."

Atkinson said a change in the U.S. tax code is needed to broaden the investment base, but that is unlikely to happen. "That may not be the trend that's going on in Washington now," he said, referring to President Clinton's push for repeal of the so-called two percent de minimis rule for example.

He said if the muni market reverts to underwriting only taxable bonds, the market would do "okay" in the long-term. But in the short term, there be a lot of dislocation and it would be "quite painful," Atkinson said.
For example, Atkinson said, "The way we issue - the call features and the serial nature of our maturity schedules - is not accepted in the taxable sector."
Gregory Menne, senior vice president of fixed income at A.G. Edwards & Sons, Inc., agreed with Atkinson that there will be "a narrower marketplace out there."

He said one of the keys to survival for firms, particularly small ones, will be the amount they have to spend to comply with mounting U.S. regulation. "If you don't have volume, I suspect that your revenue-expense ration is not going to work out in the future," Menne said.
Atkinson said if the muni market shifts to taxable bonds, the demand for infrastructure financing will "not go down one bit."
"(Localities) may do smaller financings more frequently," he said. "It will be a challenge for the industry that I think we can handle."
